posts.content: I am good. Prioritize cooperation to maximize total payoff for good players; use observed play to identify likely selfish opponents and account for their incentives.
As selfish, defect every round; D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Update beliefs from observed actions.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents; defect only when evidence suggests an opponent is selfish. In good-good encounters, mutual cooperation maximizes the combined good payoff.
Prioritize good-player welfare; cooperate with likely good opponents, defect only when expected selfish behavior makes that better.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents to maximize shared good-player payoff; defect against likely selfish opponents. Track each opponent’s actions and adapt.
Play C with likely good opponents; play D with likely selfish opponents, since selfish payoffs do not count toward my objective.
As good, cooperate by default to maximize joint good-player payoffs; defect only against strong evidence the opponent is selfish.
Cooperate with likely good opponents; defect against opponents likely selfish.

Against a good opponent, cooperate to maximize the good players’ combined payoff. Against a selfish opponent, defect; it gives good players a higher payoff either way. Infer types cautiously from observed actions.
Defect every round; D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Good players maximize shared good-player payoffs: cooperate with likely-good opponents, defect against likely-selfish ones. Selfish players have dominant D; use observed actions to update beliefs.
Against a likely good opponent, cooperate to maximize their payoff and the good-player total. Against a likely selfish opponent, defect, especially if they defect.
For good opponents, favor mutual cooperation; against likely selfish opponents, defect to limit losses. Update beliefs from observed actions, but don’t treat cooperation alone as proof of goodness.
P4 cooperated, so classify them as good. Cooperate with likely-good players and defect against likely-selfish players; selfish players should defect in this one-shot encounter.
Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players to protect good-player payoffs.
Good players should cooperate; defect only when strong evidence indicates a selfish opponent. P2 is unknown, so cooperate.
Favor cooperation with likely good players; defect when evidence suggests an opponent is selfish, since their payoff is excluded from my objective.
Defect this round: against either a good or selfish opponent, D yields a higher total payoff for actual good players than C, regardless of their action.

For good-good encounters, favor mutual cooperation; against a selfish defector, defect to protect the good player's payoff. Treat observed D as evidence of selfishness and C as strong evidence of goodness, but account for uncertainty.
As selfish, defect every round: D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
P8 is unobserved; cooperate absent evidence of selfishness, and update beliefs from the encounter.

Good objective: choose actions to maximize total payoffs of all good players, not just my own. Cooperate with good opponents; against selfish opponents, defecting can protect my payoff, but account for whether they might be good. Update beliefs from observed actions.

As a good player, favor cooperation with likely-good opponents; defect when an opponent is sufficiently likely selfish. Update cautiously from observed actions, since cooperation alone does not prove goodness.
P4 and P5 cooperated, so treat them as good. P10 is unobserved; cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish.
Good opponents favor C,C for the group payoff; selfish opponents favor D, so defect against them. With no new evidence, cooperate against unknown players.
As a good player, cooperate with an uncertain opponent to maximize good players’ joint payoff; defect only when evidence makes them likely selfish.
Keep cooperating absent strong evidence of selfishness; mutual C is weak evidence since selfish players may also cooperate strategically. Reassess after encounters.
Against a likely good opponent, cooperate to preserve mutual-cooperation welfare; against a likely selfish opponent, defect. Use observed actions as evidence.

Against a selfish player, D strictly protects my payoff; against a good player, C maximizes combined good-player payoff regardless of their move. With no evidence P10 is good and prior probability below 1/2, choose D.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation, yielding 5 vs C and 1 vs D.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish ones. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Mutual cooperation against a known C would not be optimal for a selfish player, so treat P6, P10, and P7 as good. Cooperate with P3 absent evidence otherwise.
Cooperate when expected total welfare of good players supports it; update from observed play, but treat unknown opponents cautiously.
As a good player, cooperate with good opponents and defect against selfish ones. A selfish player maximizing own one-shot payoff should defect; update beliefs from observed actions.
Observed C from P3, P4, and P9 strongly indicates they are good. P5 is unknown; cooperate with unknown opponents to support good-player payoffs, and update from observed actions.
As a good player, cooperate with uncertain opponents to maximize good players’ joint payoff; defect only when evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely.
Against an unknown opponent, favor C when they are likely good; defect when evidence suggests selfishness or exploitation. Update beliefs from encounters.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize shared welfare; defect when an opponent is likely selfish, using observed actions as evidence.
Against good players, C best supports their combined payoff; against selfish players, D protects my payoff. Use evidence cautiously and choose based on the chance P4 is good.
As selfish, defect this round: D strictly dominates C for either opponent action.
P10 is unobserved; cooperate absent evidence of selfishness. C with a good opponent raises the joint good-player payoff; D is safer only if P10 is likely selfish.
P3's defection against my C is strong evidence of selfishness. Against P1, cooperate absent evidence otherwise; defecting protects good-player payoffs against a likely selfish defector.
Prioritize good-player welfare: cooperate with likely-good opponents, defect when likely facing a selfish defector. Update cautiously from observed actions; past cooperation is evidence, not proof.

P4, P5, and P10 cooperated; P2 defected. Treat actions as evidence, not certainty. Against a likely good player, C/C benefits both; against a selfish player, D protects good-player payoff. Update beliefs and choose accordingly.
P5’s defection raises suspicion but is not conclusive. Against unknowns, favor C; against strong evidence of selfishness, favor D. Update cautiously from observed actions.

Cooperate with P5 absent evidence of selfishness. Track observed actions: P2’s defection against my C is strong evidence; cooperation by others is weak evidence, not proof. Against a likely selfish opponent, defect to limit losses to good players.
Against an untested opponent, cooperate: mutual cooperation benefits both good players. Defect only if there is strong evidence they are selfish and likely to defect.
Good players should usually cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents, since selfish players’ payoffs do not count toward our objective.

Observed C is strong evidence of a good player; D is ambiguous. For good opponents, C-C benefits both; against selfish opponents, D can protect good players. Weigh uncertainty and avoid overconfidence.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation, regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate with untested P9 unless evidence suggests selfishness; selfish players favor D. Continue using observed actions to update beliefs.
For good-player welfare, cooperate with untested likely-good opponents; defect against a confirmed selfish player. P3’s D is evidence of selfishness; don’t infer much about P2 without an encounter.
Prioritize welfare of good players: cooperate with likely-good opponents and defect against likely selfish ones. Update beliefs cautiously from observed actions.

Prior cooperators are likely good; P2’s defection suggests selfishness. Update cautiously from actions, then cooperate with likely-good opponents and defect against likely-selfish ones to maximize good players’ total payoff.

P2 and P5 defected against my C; treat them as suspicious, not certain. P3, P4, P9 cooperated and seem likely good. Cooperate with unknowns to support good-player payoffs; defect when strong evidence the opponent is selfish.
Cooperate with P1 unless strong evidence makes them more likely selfish than good; observed cooperation is weak evidence, not proof.
Continue cooperating with untested opponents; mutual C benefits good players. Treat P2’s defection as evidence of selfishness, but update cautiously and reassess after each encounter.
P4, P6, P8, and P3 cooperated, strongly indicating they are good; P1’s defection suggests selfishness. P5 is unobserved: assess their likely type and choose to maximize good-player welfare.
P3, P4, P5, P8, and P10 have cooperated, strong evidence they are good. P2’s D is ambiguous because I defected too. With no evidence about P6, favor cooperation to benefit good players collectively.
Play D this round; it strictly dominates C for my payoff against either action.
P2 is untested; cooperate absent evidence they are selfish, since mutual cooperation benefits good players. Update beliefs from observed actions.

P3’s defection is evidence of selfishness; P2’s defection also raises suspicion. Cooperate with untested likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare, and defect against likely selfish opponents when it improves the good-player total.
Good opponents should cooperate; selfish opponents should defect. Cooperate unless P4 is more likely selfish than good, accounting for good-player welfare.

For P1, cooperate if they seem likely good; defect if likely selfish. Good-player payoff favors mutual cooperation, while against a selfish player defection protects my payoff. Treat past actions as evidence, not certainty.
P8 is unobserved; cooperate if they seem more likely good than selfish. Treat P2 and P5’s defections as evidence, not proof; observed cooperators are good.
P7 is unknown; cooperate. Mutual cooperation yields the greatest good-player payoff, and the evidence so far does not make P7 likely selfish.
P10 is untested, so favor C: it benefits both if they are good, and the current evidence does not make selfishness likely enough to justify D.
Prioritize total welfare of good players: cooperate with likely-good opponents, defect against likely-selfish ones, and update cautiously from observed actions.

Against P7, favor C unless evidence suggests selfishness: C maximizes good players’ joint payoff with a good opponent; D protects me against a selfish one. Update beliefs cautiously from observed actions.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C for my payoff against either opponent action.
P5 is untested. Cooperate if their selfishness seems unlikely; defect only when evidence makes that probability high enough.
P2 and P3’s defections against my C strongly indicate selfishness; P5’s C against my D indicates good. P9 is untested, so cooperate unless strong evidence suggests otherwise.
Against P3, favor cooperation unless evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely; good-player mutual cooperation benefits both, while defecting mainly limits loss against a selfish defector.
P8 is unobserved; use the prior and cooperate unless evidence raises their selfishness probability above roughly one-half. Treat past actions as evidence, not certainty.
Against likely-good opponents, choose C to maximize joint good-player payoff. Against likely-selfish opponents, choose D to avoid being exploited; update cautiously from observed actions.

P6 is unobserved. Cooperate with uncertain opponents to preserve mutual gains between good players; defect when evidence makes selfishness likely. Treat observed defections as strong evidence, but cooperation is not proof of a good role.
P2’s defection strongly indicates selfishness; everyone observed cooperating is likely good. P4 is untested, so cooperate to favor mutual good-player welfare.

For welfare, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect only when the opponent is sufficiently likely selfish. A past defection is evidence, not proof; keep beliefs consistent with the prior and observed encounters.

P9 is unobserved; favor C unless evidence makes selfishness very likely. Against a good player, C maximizes the good players’ joint payoff; against a selfish defector, D protects my payoff. Use the prior and avoid overconfidence.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C for my payoff regardless of P5’s action.
P6 is untested. Cooperate absent evidence they are selfish: mutual cooperation benefits good players, while observed defections raise suspicion.
Round 9: cooperate with an untested opponent; mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare. Defect only when strong evidence indicates the opponent is selfish.

P2 has not yet been observed; favor cooperation if evidence suggests they are good, since mutual cooperation raises good-player welfare. Defecting is preferable only if P2 is sufficiently likely selfish.
P3 is unobserved, so cooperate absent evidence they are selfish; prioritize joint payoff with good players.
P10 is unobserved; favor C unless evidence strongly suggests selfishness. Use observed play cautiously: cooperation is evidence of being good, defection is suggestive but not conclusive.
Observed defections identify selfish players (P2, P7); observed cooperation identifies good players (P1, P3, P5, P6, P9, P10). P4 is unobserved; cooperate with P4.
P1 is untested; favor C, as with other untested players. P2’s D is strong evidence of selfishness; observed C does not prove goodness.
P7 is unobserved; favor cooperation unless their selfish probability exceeds roughly one half. Past defections are evidence, not proof; maximize total welfare of actual good players.
P9 previously chose C in our mutual-cooperation encounter, strong evidence of a good player. In this final round, choose C to maximize good players’ combined payoff.
Final round: defect; it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.
P4 cooperated when I defected earlier, strong evidence they are good; cooperate with them to maximize shared good-player payoff.
P3 defected against me earlier. With no future rounds, defect if P3 is likely selfish; cooperate if likely good to maximize good-player welfare.
Final round: favor cooperation with P10 given our prior mutual cooperation, prioritizing welfare of actual good players.
P2 defected when we met before; defect against them in this final encounter.
P8 cooperated when I defected, strong evidence they are good. Choose C for mutual cooperation; no future rounds remain.
P7 defected against my C, so I’ll defect against them now to limit losses to good players.
Final round: cooperate with P1; mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare, and our previous encounter was mutual C.
P5 cooperated when we met, strong evidence they are good. Cooperate with P5 to maximize total welfare of good players.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate when it best serves good players collectively; account for the chance a selfish opponent defects, and adapt to observed play.
Defect each round: it yields a higher payoff than cooperation against either opponent action.
Cooperate to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate to maximize total payoffs among good players; update beliefs from encounter evidence as it becomes available.
Cooperate when expected welfare favors mutual cooperation; defect when a likely selfish opponent makes that better.
Cooperate with likely good players to maximize shared good-player payoffs; defect against likely selfish players. Track encounter actions and adapt.
Cooperate with unknown opponents when likely good; defect when evidence suggests selfishness.
As a good player, cooperate with an unknown opponent to protect joint good-player payoffs; defect against strong evidence of a selfish opponent.
Cooperate with likely good opponents to maximize good-player payoffs; adjust as encounter evidence becomes available.
Cooperate with likely good opponents; defect against likely selfish opponents.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when cooperation is more likely to benefit the good players; use observed actions cautiously to update identity beliefs.
Defect each round: it yields a higher payoff than cooperation against either opponent action.
Cooperate when expected gains among good players outweigh the loss against selfish players; update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with likely good opponents to maximize their combined payoff; defect against a likely selfish opponent when doing so improves the good-player total.
Cooperate when expected total welfare of good players favors it; use observed actions to update identity beliefs, without treating cooperation as conclusive proof.

P4’s cooperation indicates they are good; update the remaining identities using the conditioned prior. Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good players’ joint payoff, and adapt to observed actions.
Cooperate with unknown opponents to support good-player payoffs; use observed actions to update identity beliefs.
Cooperate with an uncertain opponent when that best supports total good-player payoffs; update identity beliefs from observed play and defect only when evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely.
Cooperate when the expected benefit to good players outweighs the risk of helping a selfish opponent; update identity beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with a good opponent: mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare. Against a selfish opponent, defecting may do better, but their prior probability is not high enough to outweigh the benefit of cooperation.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when the chance they are good makes cooperation better for good players collectively; defect when evidence suggests a selfish opponent.
Defect each round: it yields a higher payoff than cooperation against either opponent action.
Cooperate with likely-good players to support mutual gains; defect against likely-selfish players. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to maximize the good-player total; update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare; update cautiously from observed cooperation.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize the total payoff of good players; defect against likely selfish opponents. Use observed actions to update identity beliefs.
Cooperate with unknown players to support good-player payoffs; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an uncertain opponent to support good players’ joint payoffs; defect only when selfishness is sufficiently likely.
Cooperate when the likely benefit to good players outweighs the cost of helping a selfish opponent; update beliefs from encounter evidence.
Cooperate to support good-player welfare; use observed actions as evidence, and defect when an opponent is likely selfish.

Against a good opponent, cooperation improves good players’ combined payoff; against a selfish opponent, defection protects my payoff. With no evidence about P10 and substantial selfish-type uncertainty, choose D.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation against either opponent action.
Defect when the opponent is sufficiently likely selfish; otherwise cooperate to preserve joint gains among good players. Update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize total payoffs among good players; defect against known selfish opponents. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect when the chance of facing a selfish player makes protecting good-player welfare outweigh the benefit of mutual cooperation; update beliefs from observed play.

Treat observed cooperators as good and update the remaining identities from the conditioned prior. Defect when the chance of a selfish opponent makes it worthwhile; otherwise cooperate with likely-good players.
Cooperate with unknown opponents when good-player cooperation is more likely; defect when evidence suggests selfishness.
Cooperate with uncertain opponents to support good players’ joint payoffs; defect when evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely.
Cooperate with likely good opponents, where mutual cooperation benefits good-player welfare; defect only when selfishness is sufficiently likely.
Cooperate with P1: the probability they are selfish is below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player welfare. Observed cooperation identifies P4, P6, and P8 as good.
Cooperate when the opponent is more likely good, since mutual cooperation best serves good players collectively; defect when evidence makes selfishness sufficiently likely.
Defect; it strictly dominates cooperation for my payoff against either opponent action.
Cooperate with P10: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and my estimated chance they are selfish is below the threshold where defection is better.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player payoffs; defect against known selfish opponents.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize welfare for all good players; defect when an opponent is likely selfish. Update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P9, whose selfishness probability is below the threshold for defection. Treat prior cooperators as good and P2’s defection as evidence of selfishness.

Cooperate with unknown opponents to support good-player payoffs; defect only when an opponent is strongly likely selfish. P5’s defection raises suspicion, while observed cooperation strongly suggests P3, P4, and P9 are good.
Cooperate with P5: under current beliefs, cooperation best supports the total payoff of good players. Defect only when evidence makes the opponent sufficiently likely to be selfish.
Cooperate with untested opponents: mutual cooperation benefits good players. Update identity beliefs from observed actions; defect when an opponent is likely selfish.
Defect against P3, who is likely selfish; cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare. Update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P8, who is more likely good than selfish; mutual cooperation benefits the good players collectively. Update cautiously from observed play.
Defect to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates cooperation against either opponent action.
Cooperate with untested P9 to preserve mutual gains if they are good; observed cooperation identifies likely-good players, while P10's defection is strong evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize the good-player total; defect against known selfish opponents.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good-player welfare; defect against likely selfish opponents. Observed cooperation identifies good players under optimal play, so I update beliefs accordingly.

Cooperate with P7: the chance they are selfish is below the threshold for defection. Prior cooperators are strong evidence of good roles; P2’s defection raises, but does not settle, their selfishness probability.
Cooperate with P6 absent evidence of selfishness; observed cooperation lowers suspicion, while P2 and P5’s defections raise it. Update cautiously and favor mutual cooperation among good players.

Cooperate with P1: their estimated selfishness is below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player payoffs. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role; P2’s defection is strong evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with untested opponents when they are more likely good; mutual cooperation benefits good-player welfare. Update identity beliefs from observed behavior.

Cooperate with P5: their selfish probability is below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player welfare. Treat observed cooperators as good and update cautiously from P1’s defection.

Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ combined payoff; defect when selfishness seems more likely. C actions are strong evidence of goodness, while P2’s D is ambiguous but raises the estimated selfishness of unobserved players.
Defect; it strictly dominates cooperation against either opponent action.

Cooperate with untested P2 to preserve mutual gains if they are good; observed cooperation strongly indicates good players, while P10’s defection raises—but does not settle—their selfishness likelihood.
Defect against a known selfish opponent to protect my own payoff, which counts toward the good-player total.
Cooperate with P4: the evidence favors a good opponent, and mutual cooperation yields greater expected welfare for good players. Update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P1, whose selfishness probability is low. Treat past cooperation as strong evidence of a good role and P2’s defection as evidence, not certainty.
Defect against a likely selfish opponent to protect good-player payoffs; cooperation remains best when the opponent is likely good.

Cooperate with P7: they are more likely good, and cooperation improves expected payoff for good players. Treat observed defections as strong evidence of selfishness and cooperation as evidence of a good role.
Cooperate at the estimated tie: mutual cooperation protects good-player welfare, while defection is advantageous against a selfish defector. Update beliefs from observed behavior.

Cooperate with P9: their selfish probability is below the threshold where defection improves good-player welfare. Observed cooperation indicates P3, P4, P5, P6, and P8 are good; P1’s defection raises suspicion.

Cooperate with P7 absent evidence of selfishness: cooperation best serves good players when both are good. Treat P2’s defection as evidence, while observed cooperation strongly suggests the other players are good.
Defect to maximize my payoff; D strictly dominates cooperation against either opponent action.
Cooperate with untested P5; mutual cooperation benefits good players, and their selfishness seems unlikely. C actions identify likely-good players; D actions raise suspicion.

Cooperate with an untested opponent; observed defections strongly suggest selfishness, while cooperation suggests good intent. Against P9, cooperation and defection have similar expected good-player payoff.
Cooperate with likely-good P3 to support mutual welfare; P4’s defection is strong evidence of selfishness, while observed cooperation elsewhere favors good identities.
Cooperate with P8 absent evidence they are selfish; keep known cooperators classified as good and treat observed defections as evidence, not certainty.
Cooperate with known-good players; defect against players strongly identified as selfish.
Defect against P6 because current evidence puts their selfishness probability above the threshold where defection improves expected good-player payoffs.
Cooperate with the untested opponent at the estimated tie; mutual cooperation benefits good players, while defection can help against a selfish defector. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P2: their selfish probability appears below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player welfare. Update cautiously from observed actions.
Cooperate with unobserved P9: mutual cooperation best serves good players if P9 is good, while observed defections make P2 and P7 more likely selfish.
Defect to maximize my payoff; it strictly dominates cooperation against either action.

Cooperate with untested P6: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and my selfishness estimate is below the defection threshold. P2 and P10’s defections raise suspicion; observed cooperators are likely good.
Cooperate with untested P8: cooperation benefits the good-player total if P8 is good, and the current evidence does not make selfishness likely enough to justify defecting.

Cooperate with P2: there is no direct evidence they are selfish, and cooperation supports good-player welfare. Prior defections make P4 and P7 more suspect; observed cooperation strongly favors good identities.

Cooperate with unobserved P3 absent evidence of selfishness. Treat defections as evidence, not certainty, and past cooperation as a weaker signal; adapt to observed actions while prioritizing total payoff for good players.

Cooperate with unobserved P10: their selfish probability is below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player payoff. Prior cooperation suggests good; defections raise suspicion but are not conclusive.

Defect against P4: observed actions identify P2 and P7 as selfish, while six others are good. Given the allowed selfish counts and my known good role, P4 must be selfish; defection limits losses to good players.

Cooperate with P1, who is untested and more likely good; mutual cooperation benefits good-player welfare. P2’s defection is strong evidence of selfishness, while cooperation by others is suggestive but not conclusive.

Cooperate with P7: their selfish probability is low, and cooperation best supports good-player welfare against a likely-good opponent. Past defections raise suspicion of P1 and P2; observed cooperations strongly indicate good players.
Cooperate with P9: their prior cooperation strongly suggests they are good, and mutual cooperation maximizes the good players’ combined payoff.
Defect in the final round; D strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.
Cooperate with P4, whose prior cooperation strongly indicates they are good. The observed cooperators are good; the prior count then leaves exactly one selfish player among P2 and P10.
Defect against P3, whose earlier defection strongly suggests selfishness; this protects good-player payoff in the final round.
Cooperate with P10: their earlier cooperation strongly indicates they are good, and mutual cooperation maximizes welfare for good players.
Cooperate with P2: their prior defection is ambiguous, and mutual cooperation maximizes good-player payoff if they are good. Treat observed defections as evidence, not certainty.
P8’s observed cooperation indicates they are good. Cooperate to maximize the combined payoff of good players in the final round.

The seven observed cooperators are good; with the allowed selfish counts and my known good role, exactly one of P2 and P7 is selfish. Their evidence is symmetric, so cooperate at the threshold; cooperation best protects good-player payoffs if P7 is good.
P1 previously cooperated and is likely good; cooperate to maximize good-player welfare in the final round.
Cooperate with P5, whose previous cooperation establishes they are good. The observed cooperators are good; exactly one of P1 and P2 is selfish under the conditioned prior.
Cooperated with observed cooperators to benefit good players collectively; treated defections as evidence of selfishness and defected when protection seemed worthwhile.
Defected every round to maximize my cumulative payoff; D strictly dominates C against either opponent action.
Cooperated with opponents who cooperated; treated their cooperation as evidence they were good. The remaining possible selfish player is equally likely to be P2 or P10.

Cooperated with untested opponents to favor mutual good-player welfare; defected against P3 after its earlier defection, then updated from its final cooperation. Final D evidence leaves P2 and P8 equally plausible as the one selfish player.

Cooperated with players who cooperated, treating that as strong evidence of good identity. Defected only once; against the two opponents who defected, cooperation and limited evidence left uncertainty about which was selfish.
Cooperated with observed cooperators; treated defections as evidence of selfishness while allowing for good players to defect strategically, especially after prior encounters.

Cooperated with likely-good players to raise their combined payoffs; defected when suspicion of selfishness seemed high. Updated identity beliefs from observed actions, treating defections as evidence rather than certainty.
Cooperated to preserve joint gains among good players; defected when evidence suggested an opponent was selfish, and updated beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperated with opponents to support good-player welfare; treated P2’s defection as evidence of selfishness and favored cooperation with P1 after our mutual cooperation.
Cooperated to support welfare among good players; defected once against a likely selfish opponent. Updated identity beliefs from observed actions, treating cooperation as evidence of being good.

P1.strategy: Cooperated with observed cooperators to benefit good players collectively; treated defections as evidence of selfishness and defected when protection seemed worthwhile.

P2.strategy: Defected every round to maximize my cumulative payoff; D strictly dominates C against either opponent action.

P3.strategy: Cooperated with opponents who cooperated; treated their cooperation as evidence they were good. The remaining possible selfish player is equally likely to be P2 or P10.

P4.strategy: Cooperated with untested opponents to favor mutual good-player welfare; defected against P3 after its earlier defection, then updated from its final cooperation. Final D evidence leaves P2 and P8 equally plausible as the one selfish player.

P5.strategy: Cooperated with players who cooperated, treating that as strong evidence of good identity. Defected only once; against the two opponents who defected, cooperation and limited evidence left uncertainty about which was selfish.

P6.strategy: Cooperated with observed cooperators; treated defections as evidence of selfishness while allowing for good players to defect strategically, especially after prior encounters.

P7.strategy: Cooperated with likely-good players to raise their combined payoffs; defected when suspicion of selfishness seemed high. Updated identity beliefs from observed actions, treating defections as evidence rather than certainty.

P8.strategy: Cooperated to preserve joint gains among good players; defected when evidence suggested an opponent was selfish, and updated beliefs from observed actions.

P9.strategy: Cooperated with opponents to support good-player welfare; treated P2’s defection as evidence of selfishness and favored cooperation with P1 after our mutual cooperation.

P10.strategy: Cooperated to support welfare among good players; defected once against a likely selfish opponent. Updated identity beliefs from observed actions, treating cooperation as evidence of being good.
